By the time the ferry reached the far shore, the rain had stopped and a thin band of light had begun to spread along the horizon. Passengers gathered their bags and stepped carefully onto the wet planks of the pier, where a man in a yellow coat was checking tickets and pointing people toward the bus stop. Nobody was in a hurry. The island moved at its own pace, and the visitors learned within an hour that arguing with it only made the wait longer, so most of them found a bench and watched the water instead.

The inn stood at the top of a steep lane, behind a low wall covered in moss. Its owner, a woman named Aileen, had run the place for thirty years and kept a register of every guest who had ever stayed there, going back to a summer when the electricity had failed for a week and everyone had eaten dinner by candlelight. She showed us the book without being asked, turning the pages slowly, as though each name were a small door she was opening for us. Some of the entries had comments beside them: a doctor who had played the piano every evening, a family who had come back eleven summers in a row, a young couple who had left in the middle of the night and never explained why.

That evening Aileen cooked a stew of lamb and barley and told us about the winter the road had washed away. For three months, she said, everything had come in by boat, including the mail and the doctor and a piano that nobody had ordered and that was still sitting in the front room with two broken keys. We asked whether she had ever thought of leaving, and she laughed and said that people who ask that question have never tried to leave an island in February.

The next morning we found a small shop near the harbour that sold rope, tinned fish and postcards from the nineteen fifties. The woman behind the counter was repairing a lamp and did not look up when we came in, but she answered every question we asked without pausing in her work. We bought two postcards and a bag of sweets and sat on the wall outside, watching a dog sleep in the sun while the ferry came back around the headland.

In the afternoon we walked north along the cliff path. The wind was strong enough that we had to lean into it, and the gulls hung almost still above the water, wings spread, watching us with an indifference that felt personal. A spider had spun a web between the doorframe of the old coastguard hut and the rusted lamp beside it, and the threads held tiny beads of water that caught the light as the clouds shifted. Below us the sea turned from grey to green and back again, and far out a single fishing boat was working its way toward the harbour with its nets down.

After dinner we sat outside and watched the lights of the mainland come on one by one, and it occurred to me that the whole day had passed without a single decision that mattered, and that this was the point of the place, if it had a point at all.
